source.title: On the Practice of Scaling Search Conversion Rate Prediction
source.authors: James Pak; Jyun-Yu Jiang; Fan Zhang; Sen-Zhang Wang; Taekmin Kim; Henry Tsai; V. Rajaram; Jue-Xin Lin; Mohit Singh; Alessandro Magnani; Johnny Chen; Qian Zhao; Rao Fu; Zhi-Rong Liang; Jordan Gilliland; W. Jiao

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws for language models, but its experiments concern search conversion-rate prediction models and mAP, not held-out language-model pretraining loss or the other specified claim measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling results for CVR models, but they do not directly test any listed version: the models and outcome measure differ from those specified. It also refers to language-model scaling laws in the discussion and related work; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: All experiments scale search CVR ranking models (DCNv2, MaskNet, Transformer, RankMixer) and measure relative offline mAP. None reports held-out language-model pretraining loss. The data-scaling result is a log-linear fit of mAP gain, not a power law in loss. So it is a related construct in a different system and is not recorded as testing V5 or any other version. LLM scaling laws are cited only as motivation and in related work.
record.authors_conclusion:
Mostly correct. The authors also stress several further points:
(1) Backbone and scaling-factor choice is crucial; tuned MaskNet beats sequence models per FLOP.
(2) Backbone, embedding and data effects are largely independent and additive.
(3) Single optimized backbones beat DHEN ensembles at equal FLOPs.
(4) Warmstarting and inference optimizations make scaled models deployable.
(5) The deployed model achieved +2.1% offline mAP and +2.6% online conversion rate.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales search CVR prediction models and evaluates mAP; it does not apply the original language-model scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that scaling effectiveness varies by backbone and scaling factor; cross width and Transformer sequence length are particularly effective in their tested setup. Data-scaling trends are described as consistent across tested backbones.

fits_no_version.finding: For MaskNet on search CVR, mAP gain rises log-linearly with training-data duration (fit roughly 0.39ln(days)−1.29), with diminishing returns. This is mAP, not loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In search CVR ranking models, offline mAP improves roughly log-linearly with training-data duration.

fits_no_version.finding: Gains depend strongly on which factor is scaled. Cross width beats deep width, and Transformer sequence length beats layers and heads, which give no gain. Item-ID embedding dimension helps more than a 10x vocabulary; query embeddings plateau and title embeddings give no gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In CVR models, which architectural factor is scaled matters a great deal; some factors yield zero mAP gain. This contrasts in spirit with the LM 'shape matters little' finding.

fits_no_version.finding: Data, backbone and embedding scaling gains are roughly additive (+0.47%, +0.10%, +0.13% individually vs +0.74% combined). Relative model rankings hold across training-data durations (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In CVR ranking models, gains from different scaling dimensions are approximately additive, and model rankings on small data transfer to larger data.

record.problems: The reported scaling outcomes are for search CVR mAP rather than held-out language-model loss. The data-scaling curve is presented as a figure, and the extracted fit text has an unclear sign before 1.29. The paper does not report uncertainty estimates for these results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports many individual backbone-factor settings; these were not transcribed separately because they concern CVR mAP rather than any listed claim measure. Figure 5 and the remaining scaling plots are likewise not separately catalogued.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fitting of loss laws on small LM runs to predict larger runs. The data-size transfer of model rankings (Fig. 5) concerns CVR mAP rankings, not loss extrapolation.
No LM shape-versus-loss comparison at fixed parameters.
Studies CVR recommendation scaling but measures mAP, not training or held-out loss. No power-law fit of loss is reported.
No LM downstream performance versus LM scale or loss.
No analysis of how fitting choices affect LM exponents or allocations.

record.verdict_notes: Borderline for V5 (new setting), but the measure is a ranking metric (mAP), not loss. The authors describe their curves as log-linear mAP gains, not loss power laws, so the study is kept as not testing. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Table 1 per-factor values are only summarized in R11, which is acceptable since no version is affected.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss of language models against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit loss curves on small language-model runs and compare predictions with larger runs.
It does not identify a loss-minimising parameter-and-token allocation for a fixed compute budget.
It does not compare language-model architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Although it studies scaling in CVR prediction, it does not test whether the specified loss power law transfers to other modalities or training regimes.
It does not test downstream-task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.
It does not assess how language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on fitting choices.

rows.subject: MaskNet
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-data duration and measured mAP gain.
rows.value: The paper describes the trend as predictable and log-linear; the plotted fit is given as “y = 0.39ln(x) 1.29” (the sign before 1.29 is unclear in the extracted text).
rows.note: This is CVR-model mAP, not language-model held-out loss.
rows.check: The fit's missing sign is almost certainly a minus: 0.39ln(x)−1.29 gives about 0.5 at 100 days and 1.13 at 500 days, matching the plotted 0–1.2% range. The value should read 'y = 0.39ln(x) − 1.29 (sign inferred)'.
